questions.q: What does a scalar user-defined function return?
options: A cursor over a result set
A full table with rows and columns
A single value of the declared RETURNS type
Nothing — it only runs side effects
questions.explain: A scalar UDF is declared RETURNS <type> and computes exactly one value, just like a built-in function such as LEN().

questions.q: Why can calling a scalar UDF on every row of a large query hurt performance?
options: The optimizer treats it as a black box and invokes it once per row, which can block a parallel plan
SQL Server converts every scalar UDF call into a full table scan automatically
Scalar UDFs can only be called one time per session
Scalar UDFs are not allowed to reference columns, only constants
questions.explain: Row-by-row invocation is the well-known scalar UDF performance trap — it can also degrade cardinality estimates and push the optimizer toward a serial plan.

options: A SQL Server 2019+ (compat level 150+) optimizer feature that can fold a qualifying scalar UDF into the surrounding set-based query plan
A feature exclusive to inline table-valued functions, not scalar functions
A setting that disables scalar UDFs entirely
A way to paste the function body manually into every query that calls it
questions.explain: When a scalar UDF is simple enough to qualify, inlining removes much of the old row-by-row penalty by rewriting it as part of the normal plan.

questions.q: Which kind of scalar UDF typically does NOT qualify for inlining?
options: One that only does simple arithmetic on its parameters
One that uses TRY/CATCH, calls non-deterministic built-ins, or does its own error handling
One called from a SELECT list
One that returns a money type
questions.explain: Inlining only applies to functions simple enough to translate safely; functions with error handling or non-deterministic logic still run the old row-by-row way.

questions.q: In `CREATE FUNCTION dbo.ProductMargin(@ListPrice money, @StandardCost money) RETURNS money AS BEGIN RETURN @ListPrice - @StandardCost; END;`, how would you call it in a query?
options: SELECT ProductMargin(ListPrice, StandardCost) FROM Production.Product
SELECT * FROM dbo.ProductMargin(ListPrice, StandardCost)
CALL dbo.ProductMargin(ListPrice, StandardCost)
SELECT dbo.ProductMargin(ListPrice, StandardCost) FROM Production.Product
questions.explain: A scalar UDF is called like any schema-qualified expression — dbo.FnName(args) — directly in the SELECT list, not with FROM or CALL.
